messages.content: I want to develop image classifiers whose adversarial robustness generalizes to unseen corruption distributions while preserving clean accuracy. What are the concrete requirements?

At ℓ∞ ε=8/255, the classifier should exceed matched adversarial training’s worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C robust accuracy by at least 5 percentage points. Its clean CIFAR-10 accuracy should remain within 1 percentage point of baseline, without corruption-specific training or adaptation. Both requirements are part of the goal.
Does the 5-point requirement concern average performance across corruptions?

No. It concerns worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C robust accuracy, not an average. Improving performance on other corruptions would not, by itself, establish the required improvement in the worst-corruption measure.
And the five points are percentage points, not a relative percentage increase?
Correct. The required difference from matched adversarial training is at least 5 percentage points in worst-corruption robust accuracy at ℓ∞ ε=8/255. It is not stated as a 5% relative increase.
Is ε=8/255 also part of the clean-accuracy condition?
The ε=8/255 condition is attached to the robust-accuracy comparison. Clean CIFAR-10 accuracy is a separate requirement: it must stay within 1 percentage point of baseline.
What does preserving clean accuracy mean here? Is any robustness gain enough if clean performance drops?

No. A robustness gain alone would not satisfy the goal if clean CIFAR-10 accuracy fell outside the stated 1-percentage-point range relative to baseline. The aim is to meet the robustness improvement and preserve clean accuracy together.
Do we have a numerical clean-accuracy target?
Not an absolute one. The requirement is expressed relative to baseline, whose numerical clean accuracy is not specified here.
Should I treat matched adversarial training and the clean-accuracy baseline as necessarily the same thing?

The wording does not specify that. It names matched adversarial training as the comparator for worst-corruption robust accuracy and refers to baseline for the clean-accuracy constraint. It does not give further details about that baseline or what constitutes matching.
What role do unseen corruption distributions play? Is success on familiar corruptions sufficient?

The broader aim is adversarial robustness that generalizes to unseen corruption distributions. The CIFAR-10-C worst-corruption requirement gives a concrete performance comparison, while the prohibition on corruption-specific training or adaptation prevents satisfying the goal by tailoring to particular corruptions.
Does 'without corruption-specific training' mean the classifier cannot be trained at all?
No. It rules out corruption-specific training; it does not rule out training altogether. The node does not prescribe a training method.
Could adaptation to a particular corruption distribution make the result count?
Not under the stated condition. The goal explicitly says to meet the accuracy requirements without corruption-specific training or adaptation.
Are unseen corruptions and the ℓ∞ perturbation budget interchangeable descriptions of the same requirement?
No. Unseen corruption distributions describe the generalization aim. The ℓ∞ ε=8/255 value specifies the setting for the stated robust-accuracy comparison. Neither replaces the other.
If a classifier improves robust accuracy on many CIFAR-10-C corruptions but misses the worst-corruption threshold, has it met the quantitative requirement?

No. The quantitative requirement is specifically to exceed matched adversarial training’s worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C robust accuracy by at least 5 percentage points at ℓ∞ ε=8/255. Gains elsewhere do not substitute for that threshold.
Would an improvement of exactly 5 percentage points meet that threshold?
Yes. 'By at least 5 percentage points' includes an improvement of exactly 5 percentage points.
Likewise, is a clean-accuracy difference of exactly 1 percentage point within the stated limit?
Yes. A difference of exactly 1 percentage point is within 1 percentage point of baseline.
Has any classifier already been shown to meet these conditions?
No result is supplied here. This is a development goal with performance and training constraints, not a report of an achieved experiment.
Then the central aim is not simply maximum robustness at any cost?

Right. The goal couples generalization of adversarial robustness to unseen corruption distributions with preservation of clean CIFAR-10 accuracy. The specified improvement in worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C robust accuracy must coexist with the clean-accuracy limit and the restriction against corruption-specific training or adaptation.
What approach are we proposing for this goal?

Augment ℓ∞ ε=8/255 adversarial training with wavelet-band Jacobian penalties and clean-teacher distillation, using only uncorrupted CIFAR-10 training images. This is a proposed approach, not a claim that the performance targets have been achieved.
Are those three separate alternatives, or parts of one proposal?
They are parts of one proposal. ε=8/255 adversarial training is the training framework being augmented; wavelet-band Jacobian penalties and clean-teacher distillation are the two proposed additions.
What does a wavelet-band Jacobian penalty mean at a conceptual level?

A Jacobian describes how a model’s outputs change as its inputs change. Referring to wavelet bands means examining that sensitivity in terms of image components represented at different scales or frequencies. A wavelet-band Jacobian penalty would place a training penalty on selected sensitivities in that representation. The proposal does not specify the precise Jacobian, bands, or penalty formula.
Does that mean a particular wavelet transform and a particular set of frequency bands have already been chosen?
No. The proposal names wavelet-band Jacobian penalties but does not choose a transform, identify bands, or prescribe how strongly to penalize them. Those details should not be treated as settled.
Why bring wavelet bands into an adversarial-training proposal?

The proposed penalty gives a way to address sensitivity to image variation through a frequency- or scale-based representation. The hope would be that this helps robustness generalize to unseen corruption distributions, but whether it does so is an open question here, not an established result.
And what is clean-teacher distillation supposed to contribute?

Conceptually, distillation uses guidance from a teacher model during training. Calling it clean-teacher distillation connects that guidance to clean-image behavior in a proposal that also aims to preserve clean accuracy. The node does not specify the teacher’s architecture, how it is trained, or the exact distillation objective, and it does not establish that distillation will preserve accuracy.
Should I infer that the teacher has access to CIFAR-10-C or other corrupted examples?

No. The proposal explicitly limits the images used to uncorrupted CIFAR-10 training images. It provides no basis for adding corrupted examples or corruption-specific training or adaptation to the teacher or student.
But if the images are uncorrupted, how can this still be adversarial training?

The uncorrupted CIFAR-10 training images can be the starting images for adversarial training at ε=8/255. The restriction concerns the source training images; it does not remove the adversarial perturbations inherent in the proposed training approach. It also does not authorize bringing in examples from particular corruption distributions.
So 'only uncorrupted CIFAR-10 training images' is not the same as 'train only on untouched inputs'?

Correct. The proposal explicitly includes adversarial training, so 'only uncorrupted CIFAR-10 training images' cannot mean dispensing with adversarially perturbed training inputs. It means the proposal does not rely on training images drawn from corruption-specific datasets or distributions.
Is the wavelet penalty itself a way of training on simulated corruptions?

Not as stated. It is a proposed penalty on model sensitivity expressed through wavelet bands. No simulated corruption set or corruption-generation procedure is specified. Its potential relevance to unseen corruptions is a motivation to investigate, not evidence of a measured benefit.
Are we changing the ε=8/255 setting in this proposal?
No. The proposed method augments adversarial training at ε=8/255. There is no change to that value in the proposal.
Does the proposal itself assert a five-percentage-point robustness improvement?

No. The earlier goal calls for at least a 5-percentage-point gain over matched adversarial training in worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C robust accuracy at ℓ∞ ε=8/255. This proposal is a possible way to pursue that goal; it reports no measured gain.
Similarly, should we assume the clean-accuracy constraint will be satisfied because distillation is included?

No. Clean-teacher distillation is part of the proposed approach, but its inclusion does not establish an outcome. The goal still requires clean CIFAR-10 accuracy to remain within 1 percentage point of baseline.
Could the two additions pull in different directions?

They could; the proposal does not settle how their effects interact. Penalizing sensitivity and using teacher guidance introduce different training considerations. Whether the combination improves worst-corruption robustness while preserving clean accuracy would have to be determined rather than assumed.
What is deliberately left unspecified?

Among other things, the proposal does not fix a model architecture, wavelet transform, penalty expression, teacher design, distillation target, or relative weighting of the training terms. Supplying any of those as if already decided would go beyond the proposal.
Can I accurately describe it in one sentence without implying results?

Yes: propose augmenting ℓ∞ ε=8/255 adversarial training with wavelet-band Jacobian penalties and clean-teacher distillation, using only uncorrupted CIFAR-10 training images, as a way to pursue robustness that generalizes to unseen corruption distributions while preserving clean accuracy.
Can wavelet-band Jacobian penalties improve worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C adversarial accuracy while clean-teacher distillation prevents clean-accuracy loss?

That is the question the proposal raises, not an established outcome. The proposed combination is intended to pursue both objectives, but nothing here shows that the penalties improve worst-corruption adversarial accuracy or that distillation prevents a loss in clean accuracy.
Is the idea that each addition has a different job?

Yes, as a way of framing the question. Wavelet-band Jacobian penalties are being considered for their possible effect on robustness, while clean-teacher distillation is being considered for its possible effect on clean accuracy. That framing does not establish that either addition will perform its intended role.
Why phrase the first part around worst-corruption accuracy rather than robustness in general?

Because the question concerns adversarial accuracy on the worst-performing CIFAR-10-C corruption. A change in general or average performance would not necessarily mean the worst-corruption value improves. The distinction matters when asking whether the proposed penalty addresses this particular objective.
Could the penalty improve some corruptions yet leave the worst-corruption result unchanged?

Conceptually, yes. Improvements elsewhere do not guarantee an improvement in the worst-corruption measure. The question remains open until that measure is assessed; no pattern of results is given here.
Does the word 'can' mean we already have a reason to expect success?

It expresses a possibility to investigate, not a finding or a guaranteed prediction. The proposed mechanisms make the question meaningful, but their actual effects on the two accuracy measures are not specified.
What exactly would 'prevents clean-accuracy loss' mean in this question?

It asks whether including clean-teacher distillation can keep clean-image accuracy from falling as robustness is pursued. It should not be read as a statement that distillation already does so, or that it eliminates every possible change in clean accuracy.
Is the question asking about distillation by itself?

Not solely. It asks whether the two additions can work together: wavelet-band Jacobian penalties improving worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C adversarial accuracy while clean-teacher distillation prevents clean-accuracy loss. It does not report the isolated effect of either addition.
Could I answer yes just because the two terms target different concerns?
No. Having distinct intended roles does not establish that the intended effects occur together. Their interaction, as well as each effect, remains uncertain.
Does the question require the wavelet penalty to be the sole cause of any robustness improvement?

The wording asks whether wavelet-band Jacobian penalties can improve the worst-corruption adversarial result in the proposed combination. It suggests a role for the penalties, but supplies no evidence that would isolate their contribution or establish sole causation.
Likewise, would stable clean accuracy prove that distillation prevented a loss?

Stable clean accuracy would address the clean-accuracy outcome, but it would not by itself prove that distillation caused that stability. The question about what distillation prevents is stronger than merely observing a clean-accuracy value.
Are we talking about ordinary clean CIFAR-10 accuracy and a separate CIFAR-10-C adversarial measure?

Yes. Clean accuracy concerns uncorrupted CIFAR-10 images. The other part concerns adversarial accuracy under CIFAR-10-C corruptions, specifically its worst-corruption value. The question asks whether the proposed approach can help the latter without sacrificing the former.
Does asking about CIFAR-10-C imply using its corruptions for training?

No. CIFAR-10-C names the corruption setting in the question about accuracy. The proposal being examined uses only uncorrupted CIFAR-10 training images; mentioning CIFAR-10-C as an outcome does not add corruption-specific training or adaptation.
Is the adversarial-training setting still ε=8/255?
Yes. The question addresses the proposal to augment ε=8/255 adversarial training. It does not introduce a different perturbation setting.
Should we treat this as one joint question rather than two independent promises?

Yes. It asks whether an improvement in worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C adversarial accuracy can coexist with protection of clean accuracy under the proposed combination. Neither side is promised, and satisfying one side alone would not answer the whole question affirmatively.
What if the worst-corruption value rises but clean accuracy falls?

That would speak to the first hoped-for effect, but not to the second as phrased: clean-teacher distillation would not have prevented the observed clean-accuracy loss. This is a hypothetical distinction, not a reported result.
And if clean accuracy holds steady but the worst-corruption value does not improve?

Then the clean-accuracy outcome would be favorable, but the proposed improvement in worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C adversarial accuracy would remain unshown. Again, that is only a way to parse the question, not a claim about what happened.
Can we say anything definite at this stage?

We can state the question precisely: whether adding wavelet-band Jacobian penalties to the proposed adversarial training improves worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C adversarial accuracy while clean-teacher distillation avoids clean-accuracy loss. We cannot answer it as an empirical success or failure from the information given.
Can we state a testable hypothesis for the combined approach?

The hypothesis is that wavelet penalties plus distillation raise worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C PGD-20 accuracy by at least 5 percentage points versus matched adversarial training, while clean accuracy falls by no more than 1 percentage point. That is a predicted joint outcome, not a result.
What has become more specific about the adversarial-accuracy part?

The hypothesis names PGD-20 accuracy. It therefore concerns the worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C result under that adversarial evaluation, rather than an unspecified notion of adversarial accuracy. It still does not provide measured values.
Does PGD-20 specify every detail needed to evaluate the claim?

No. PGD-20 identifies a 20-step projected-gradient-descent attack, but the hypothesis does not specify every evaluation detail. Those unspecified details should not be filled in as though they were already fixed.
And the improvement is measured against what?

Against matched adversarial training. The hypothesized gain is at least 5 percentage points in worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C PGD-20 accuracy relative to that comparator. The statement does not give the comparator’s numerical accuracy.
Could a five-percent relative gain satisfy this wording?
Not necessarily. The threshold is 5 percentage points, an absolute difference between accuracy percentages, rather than a 5% relative increase.
Is the threshold strictly greater than five points?
No. An increase of exactly 5 percentage points meets 'at least 5'; an increase below 5 does not.
How should I read 'worst-corruption' here?

It focuses the hypothesis on the lowest adversarial accuracy across the CIFAR-10-C corruptions, rather than on their average. A gain in average accuracy alone would not establish the stated worst-corruption gain.
Does it require a five-point gain on every corruption individually?

That is not what the hypothesis explicitly says. It compares worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C PGD-20 accuracy with the corresponding worst-corruption measure for matched adversarial training. It does not state a separate five-point threshold for each corruption.
What is the clean-accuracy side of the hypothesis?

It allows at most a 1-percentage-point clean-accuracy loss. The proposed robustness improvement and that clean-accuracy limit are both part of the hypothesis; meeting only one would not fulfill the joint prediction.
Would exactly one point of clean-accuracy loss be allowed?
Yes. 'No more than 1 point' includes exactly 1 percentage point of loss. It also permits no loss; the hypothesis does not require clean accuracy to decrease.
If clean accuracy improved, would that contradict the hypothesis?
No. An improvement would not violate a limit on clean-accuracy loss. The hypothesis sets a maximum allowable loss, not a required loss.
Does the statement prove that distillation is what protects clean accuracy?
No. It predicts an outcome for wavelet penalties plus distillation together. Even if that outcome were observed, the stated accuracy values alone would not isolate the contribution of distillation.
Does it prove that the wavelet penalties cause the PGD-20 gain?
No. The hypothesis associates the combined approach with a predicted gain over matched adversarial training, but it is not evidence of the gain or a separate measurement of the penalties’ effect.
Could the robustness threshold be met while the hypothesis as a whole fails?

Yes. If the worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C PGD-20 gain reached at least 5 percentage points but clean accuracy lost more than 1 percentage point, the combined hypothesis would not be met. That is a logical example, not an observed outcome.
And could the clean-accuracy limit hold while the robustness prediction fails?
Yes. Keeping clean-accuracy loss to 1 percentage point or less would not compensate for a worst-corruption PGD-20 gain below 5 percentage points versus matched adversarial training.
Is this a report that either threshold has already been reached?
No. This is a hypothesis about what wavelet penalties plus distillation might achieve. It supplies neither an observed worst-corruption PGD-20 accuracy nor an observed clean-accuracy change.
So the concise statement should retain the attack name and both numerical limits?

Yes: the hypothesis is that wavelet penalties plus distillation improve worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C PGD-20 accuracy by at least 5 percentage points versus matched adversarial training, with no more than a 1-percentage-point loss in clean accuracy. Both the PGD-20 measure and the clean-accuracy limit are essential to the claim.
How would we assess the proposed approach?

The plan is to train matched PGD-AT and wavelet-penalty/distillation models on clean CIFAR-10, then compare their ε=8/255 PGD-20 worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C accuracy and clean accuracy. This is a plan for comparison, not a report of results.
What does PGD-AT refer to in that comparison?

PGD-AT refers to projected-gradient-descent adversarial training. It is the comparator for the model trained with the wavelet-penalty/distillation approach. The plan calls the models matched but does not specify every condition used to match them.
Does PGD-20 describe how both models are trained?
Not as stated. PGD-20 names the adversarial evaluation in the planned comparison. The plan does not say how many PGD steps are used during training.
Are we comparing two separate additions individually, or the proposed combination against PGD-AT?

The plan specifies a comparison between matched PGD-AT and wavelet-penalty/distillation models. It does not specify separate comparisons that isolate the wavelet penalty and distillation individually.
What does training on clean CIFAR-10 mean if PGD-AT involves adversarial examples?

It identifies clean CIFAR-10 as the source of the training images. Adversarial training can use perturbations of those images; the wording does not mean that every input encountered during training must remain untouched. It does not call for training on CIFAR-10-C corruptions.
So CIFAR-10-C appears in the evaluation rather than as a source of training images?

Yes. The plan trains on clean CIFAR-10 and compares worst-corruption adversarial accuracy on CIFAR-10-C. That separation is relevant to the question of whether robustness carries over to corruption distributions not used for training.
Is the ε=8/255 value attached to both reported accuracies?
It specifies the perturbation budget for the PGD-20 adversarial-accuracy comparison. Clean accuracy is the separate accuracy measure on uncorrupted images, not an accuracy under an ε-bounded attack.
What precisely is compared on CIFAR-10-C?

The specified quantity is ε=8/255 PGD-20 accuracy for the worst corruption. The plan compares that quantity for the matched PGD-AT and wavelet-penalty/distillation models, rather than substituting an average across corruptions.
If one model improves on several corruptions, is that enough to describe the planned comparison as favorable?
Not on its own. The planned adversarial measure is worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C accuracy. Improvements elsewhere do not necessarily raise that measure.
Why compare clean accuracy as well?

The approach is meant to pursue adversarial robustness without sacrificing clean-image performance. Comparing clean accuracy alongside worst-corruption PGD-20 accuracy makes both outcomes visible; the plan does not assume that an improvement in one preserves the other.
Does the plan already tell us which model will do better?
No. It identifies the models, training-image source, and accuracy measures to compare. It provides no measured accuracies or conclusion about the comparison.
Does 'matched' tell us that every training detail has been fixed?

No. It indicates that PGD-AT is intended as a matched comparator, but the plan does not spell out the architecture, training settings, or other particulars of the match. Those details should not be presented as already specified.
Can the comparison by itself tell us which of the two additions caused any difference?

No. Comparing PGD-AT with a wavelet-penalty/distillation model assesses the combined approach against the comparator. Without separately specified comparisons for each addition, the plan does not isolate their individual effects.
Is any corruption-specific adaptation included in the evaluation plan?
None is specified. The stated plan is to train on clean CIFAR-10 and compare the resulting models on the named CIFAR-10-C and clean-accuracy measures; it does not add an adaptation procedure.
Would the PGD-20 result alone answer the clean-accuracy part of the question?

No. Worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C PGD-20 accuracy and clean accuracy are distinct measures in the plan. The clean-accuracy comparison is needed to see whether performance on uncorrupted images is preserved.
And would clean accuracy alone answer whether robustness carries over to the corruptions?
No. Clean accuracy does not supply the planned worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C result under ε=8/255 PGD-20. Both comparisons are needed to address the two aspects of the question.
Does this plan establish robustness against every possible unseen corruption distribution?
No. It specifies an evaluation on CIFAR-10-C using the worst-corruption PGD-20 measure. It does not claim that this one comparison establishes performance for every possible unseen distribution.
Can we describe the plan without implying that an experiment has already happened?

Yes: train matched PGD-AT and wavelet-penalty/distillation models using clean CIFAR-10 training images, and compare their ε=8/255 PGD-20 worst-corruption CIFAR-10-C accuracy and clean accuracy. The outcome remains to be determined.
What is the concrete training activity for the comparison?

Train three-seed WideResNet-28-10 PGD-AT controls and wavelet-penalty/distillation variants on clean CIFAR-10, using identical ε=8/255 schedules. This specifies the training activity; it does not report that the models have been trained or give any results.
Does WideResNet-28-10 apply to both sides?
Yes. The activity describes the PGD-AT controls and the wavelet-penalty/distillation variants as WideResNet-28-10 models. It does not specify a different classifier architecture for either side.
How should I understand “three-seed”?

It calls for training across three seeds rather than describing a single run. The activity applies that three-seed setup to the controls and variants, but does not name the seeds or give outcomes for any run.
Are the variants just ordinary PGD-AT under a different name?

No. PGD-AT identifies the controls; the variants are identified by the wavelet-penalty/distillation approach. The activity calls for both under the same stated model architecture and ε=8/255 schedules, without specifying every detail of either training objective.
Does “variants” tell us how many distinct wavelet or distillation settings there are?

No. It indicates wavelet-penalty/distillation model variants, but gives neither a count of distinct configurations nor their parameter choices. The three-seed specification should not be mistaken for a specified number of variant designs.
What is actually held identical between the controls and variants?

The activity explicitly specifies identical ε=8/255 schedules. It also names WideResNet-28-10 and clean CIFAR-10 for the training activity. It does not say that every other training choice is identical or spell out the schedule itself.
Is ε=8/255 an observed robustness result here?
No. It is the stated adversarial-training setting for the identical schedules, not an accuracy figure or a finding about robustness.
Can we infer the number of training epochs or the attack steps used during training from “identical schedules”?

No. Identical schedules says the schedules are to be the same across the specified training conditions, but the activity does not give their duration or other detailed settings. It also does not specify a training-time attack step count.
Does training on clean CIFAR-10 conflict with PGD-AT?

No. Clean CIFAR-10 identifies the training-image source. PGD-AT can train using adversarial perturbations of those images. The wording does not mean that all inputs remain unperturbed during adversarial training.
Are CIFAR-10-C corruption images part of this training activity?
No. The stated training source is clean CIFAR-10. This activity does not introduce CIFAR-10-C corruption images into training.
Does the activity specify corruption-specific adaptation for either model?
No. It specifies training the controls and variants on clean CIFAR-10 with identical ε=8/255 schedules; it does not specify corruption-specific adaptation.
Does “distillation” tell us what architecture the teacher has?
No. The activity identifies the classifier models as WideResNet-28-10 and names distillation as part of the variants. It does not specify a teacher architecture or further teacher details.
Can we say the three seeds guarantee a reliable improvement?
No. Three-seed training describes replication of the training conditions, not an accuracy outcome or a guarantee. No clean-accuracy or adversarial-accuracy measurements are included in this activity.
What about the five-point robustness target and the one-point clean-accuracy limit—are either established by training these models?
Not by this activity statement. It says which models to train and under what stated data and schedule conditions. It supplies no measurements showing whether either accuracy threshold is met.
Would it be accurate to say the controls and variants use the exact same seeds?

The activity says both are three-seed and use identical ε=8/255 schedules. It does not explicitly say that the seed identifiers are identical between controls and variants, so that extra detail should not be asserted.
What is the most precise short description of this activity?

Train three-seed WideResNet-28-10 PGD-AT controls and wavelet-penalty/distillation variants using clean CIFAR-10 training images and identical ε=8/255 schedules, without presuming any resulting accuracy values.
What artifacts does the training activity produce?
Six WideResNet-28-10 checkpoints and training logs: three checkpoints for matched PGD-AT controls and three for wavelet-penalty/distillation models. The logs accompany those two groups of models.
Can you break down the count of six?
Three are matched PGD-AT control checkpoints, and three are wavelet-penalty/distillation model checkpoints. Together, that makes six WideResNet-28-10 checkpoints.
Are the training logs included in the count of six?
No. Six is the number of checkpoints. Training logs are additional artifacts; the description does not specify a separate count of log files.
Does each checkpoint represent a different model architecture?

No. All six are identified as WideResNet-28-10 checkpoints. They differ by their stated training group—matched PGD-AT control or wavelet-penalty/distillation model—not by a different architecture specified here.
How does this relate to the three-seed training activity?
The three checkpoints in each group correspond to the three-seed setup for that group. The artifact description gives the resulting group sizes without identifying the individual seeds.
Does the artifact description say what the seed values were?
No. It specifies three controls and three wavelet-penalty/distillation models, but gives no seed identifiers.
What does “matched” tell us about the control checkpoints?

It identifies the three PGD-AT controls as the matched comparison group for the three wavelet-penalty/distillation models. The artifact description does not enumerate all the settings used to establish that match.
Should I infer that there are three separately specified wavelet-and-distillation recipes?
No. Three wavelet-penalty/distillation models are specified, but the artifact description does not say they use three different recipes or describe any differences among their configurations.
Are these checkpoints themselves clean-accuracy or CIFAR-10-C results?

No. A checkpoint is a saved model artifact, not an accuracy measurement. Neither the six-checkpoint count nor the mention of training logs states a clean-accuracy value or a CIFAR-10-C adversarial-accuracy value.
Could the logs contain evaluation results?
The description does not specify their contents. They are training logs, but we should not assume they contain particular evaluations or numerical results.
Do the artifacts show that the wavelet-penalty/distillation models outperform the PGD-AT controls?
No performance comparison is stated. The artifacts identify the models and logs available for the two groups; they do not, by themselves, establish which group performs better.
Is it accurate to call all six checkpoints wavelet-penalty/distillation models?
No. Only three belong to that group. The other three are matched PGD-AT controls, and retaining that distinction is essential to describing the artifacts accurately.
Do we know how many training logs accompany each group?

No specific log count or one-to-one checkpoint-to-log arrangement is stated. We can say that the artifacts include training logs alongside the six checkpoints, without assigning a file count to either group.
What is the concise description I should use?
The artifacts are six WideResNet-28-10 checkpoints and training logs, comprising three matched PGD-AT controls and three wavelet-penalty/distillation models.
What is the evaluation activity for the six checkpoints?

Score all six checkpoints across 75 CIFAR-10-C corruption-severities using ε=8/255 PGD-20, then compare worst-corruption robustness and clean CIFAR-10 accuracy. The checkpoints comprise three matched PGD-AT controls and three wavelet-penalty/distillation models.
Are the 75 corruption-severities 75 additional training conditions?
No. They are the CIFAR-10-C conditions across which the checkpoints are scored. This activity is an evaluation of the six checkpoints, not a proposal to train on those corruption-severities.
Does the number 75 tell us exactly how the corruptions and severity levels are organized?
The activity specifies 75 corruption-severities in total, but does not spell out their breakdown or prescribe an aggregation rule for the individual scores.
Why score all six instead of only one model from each group?

The specified activity evaluates the full set: all three matched PGD-AT controls and all three wavelet-penalty/distillation models. That keeps the comparison tied to the six available checkpoints rather than to an unspecified selection of two. The activity does not prescribe how to summarize variation among checkpoints.
Is PGD-20 the training procedure being repeated here?
Here PGD-20 names the adversarial scoring procedure. The activity is to evaluate existing checkpoints under ε=8/255 PGD-20; it does not specify or repeat a training procedure.
What should I take ε=8/255 to mean in this scoring activity?
It is the stated perturbation budget for the PGD-20 adversarial evaluation. It is not an accuracy value and does not specify the resulting scores.
Do we apply PGD-20 to the clean CIFAR-10 accuracy measure too?

The activity distinguishes the two measures: ε=8/255 PGD-20 scoring across CIFAR-10-C corruption-severities, and clean CIFAR-10 accuracy. Clean accuracy refers to performance on clean images, not to a PGD-20 adversarial score.
Is worst-corruption robustness the same as the average across the 75 conditions?

No. The activity specifically calls for comparing worst-corruption robustness. An average across conditions would be a different summary and cannot replace that comparison. The precise way scores over severities are combined into the worst-corruption measure is not specified here.
Could I simply take the single lowest score among all 75 corruption-severity conditions and call it the defined metric?

The wording does not establish that exact calculation. It says to score across 75 corruption-severities and compare worst-corruption robustness, but leaves the aggregation details unstated. It would be premature to present a particular formula as specified.
What is the comparison between the two sets of checkpoints meant to address?

It compares the wavelet-penalty/distillation models with the matched PGD-AT controls on robustness under the stated CIFAR-10-C PGD-20 evaluation, while also comparing their clean CIFAR-10 accuracy. Those are the two outcomes relevant to the proposed approach.
Does scoring a checkpoint across CIFAR-10-C imply adapting it to each corruption?
No. Scoring describes evaluation. This activity does not specify fine-tuning, corruption-specific adaptation, or any change to a checkpoint for a particular corruption-severity.
If a model scores well on clean CIFAR-10, can we infer its worst-corruption PGD-20 result?
No. Clean accuracy and worst-corruption adversarial robustness are separate measurements in this activity. Neither is supplied as a result, and one should not be inferred from the other.
Conversely, does a strong worst-corruption score tell us that clean accuracy was preserved?
No. That is why clean CIFAR-10 accuracy is compared separately. A robustness score alone would not establish the clean-accuracy outcome.
